title: WhatsApp Prekey Bundle Side Channel
html:
WhatsApp Prekey Bundle Depletion and Refill Side Channel

WhatsApp stores an identity key, a signed prekey and a reserve of one-time prekeys for each device. Fetching a device's bundle consumes one server-held one-time prekey even if the requester sends no message. This gives an attacker with a WhatsApp account and the target phone number a server-side probe, distinct from client delivery-receipt timing. A missing one-time prekey also weakens forward secrecy for the initial messages of a newly established session; it does not expose plaintext by itself.[1][2]

Inspect a target's device bundles

The Prekey Pogo artifact pairs as a WhatsApp companion session and supports manual device and prekey queries. Pair it with a test account, then use its interactive target, devices, prekey (primary device) and combine (all devices) commands. The released artifact deliberately omits automated depletion and server-clogging functions.[1][3]

git clone https://github.com/sbaresearch/prekey-pogo
cd prekey-pogo
./setup.sh
go run .

For each response, record the device JID, bundle timestamp t, signed-prekey ID skey.id, and whether the one-time key.id is present. Device ID 0 is the phone; nonzero IDs are companions. On the implementations tested in the paper, the initial signed-prekey ID also distinguishes some clients: Android starts at 0, iOS and macOS use a random value, and WhatsApp Web and Windows Desktop start at 1. Treat this as an implementation fingerprint, not an immutable protocol rule.[1]

Turn refills into an online-status oracle

First calibrate on a device you control: repeatedly request its bundle until the server stops returning a one-time key, noting the last timestamp and key IDs. For a target device, repeat the depletion and re-query after a controlled interval: a new one-time key and advanced bundle timestamp indicate that the device uploaded a fresh batch. In the reported WhatsApp tests, the server prompted a refill below 11 remaining keys and clients uploaded 812 new keys. Apply the procedure per device JID to distinguish a phone from companions. A delayed refill only suggests that a device is offline: background scheduling, network loss and client-specific refill latency can produce the same observation. Unlike a receipt RTT, this probe does not require a delivered ciphertext or a victim-side acknowledgment.[1][2]

Each query consumes a one-time key, so a sustained oracle requires a custom client capable of repeated prekey retrieval; the public artifact only demonstrates manual queries. Keeping the reserve empty can cause other users to establish new sessions without a one-time prekey. That reduces forward secrecy for initial messages until a fresh ratchet step, but exploiting recorded ciphertext additionally requires access to the E2EE ciphertext and later compromise of the relevant long- and medium-term private keys. Existing established sessions are not automatically downgraded.[1][2][3]

References

  • [1] Prekey Pogo: Investigating Security and Privacy Issues in WhatsApp's Handshake Mechanism
  • [2] The X3DH Key Agreement Protocol
  • [3] Prekey Pogo artifacts
